analysis.one_liner: Closes fracking loopholes in federal water, air, and waste laws and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved beyond committee referral and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed exemptions that let oil and gas drilling — including fracking — avoid parts of the Safe Drinking Water Act, Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, and hazardous waste rules. It required companies to disclose the chemicals they inject underground, replace water supplies their operations contaminate, and follow federal fracking rules on public lands. It was introduced with 4 cosponsors, referred to three committees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking and drilling operations, especially those whose wells and drinking water are at risk of contamination from injected fluids and produced water. The bill would have given them required baseline water testing, public disclosure of the chemicals used underground, replacement of contaminated or depleted water supplies, and new federal limits on air pollutants like hydrogen sulfide near oil and gas wells.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking and drilling operations

how_it_helps.text: Requires oil and gas operators under federal leases to replace the water supply of anyone whose source water is contaminated, diminished, or interrupted by drilling, fracking, or production, and to submit a water management plan before drilling permits are approved.

Ends the exemption that keeps fracking fluids outside the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection rules, and requires operators to disclose the chemicals, chemical constituents, and volumes injected — with that information posted publicly — and strips trade-secret protection from chemical identities, concentrations, and health and safety data.

Restores permitting for stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations by removing the regulatory exclusion created in 2005, and directs a federal study of stormwater contamination near drilling areas.

Adds hydrogen sulfide to the Clean Air Act's list of hazardous air pollutants and covers oil and gas wells as sources, removing the Clean Air Act exemption that had kept aggregated oil and gas emissions from being regulated as a single major source.

Directs the EPA to determine within one year whether drilling fluids and produced waters are hazardous waste and to regulate them accordingly, and requires groundwater monitoring at facilities receiving those wastes.
Requires the Bureau of Land Management to issue fracking rules for federal lands within one year and, until then, re-applies the 2015 federal fracking rule that the prior administration had repealed.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and fracking service companies would bear the costs: chemical disclosure and baseline water testing, compliance with underground injection permits, stormwater permits, air emissions controls for hydrogen sulfide, hazardous waste handling for drilling fluids and produced water, and water replacement obligations. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through higher fuel prices, and industry argued state regulators were better positioned than federal agencies to oversee drilling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and fracking firms

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant compliance costs on oil and gas producers — new permits, disclosure, waste handling, and water replacement obligations — which the industry argued would raise production costs and could be passed on to consumers through higher fuel prices; reclassifying produced water as potentially hazardous waste would also affect disposal capacity nationwide.

The bill consolidates authority over drilling practices at the federal level, which runs against the long-standing arrangement in which states directly regulate oil and gas operations on most private land; opponents argued state regulators are closer to local conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is concrete and localized: people living near wells get testing, disclosure, and water replacement, and the public gets federal fracking standards on public lands for the first time since the 2015 rule was repealed. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and, indirectly, on energy consumers. The disclosure and drinking-water provisions are straightforward protections; the air and hazardous-waste provisions would require substantial new EPA rulemaking on tight deadlines. On balance the bill is designed to protect water and health at real cost to drillers, which is exactly the trade the industry fought to avoid.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to four subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on March 5, 2020, with three Democratic cosponsors (Reps. Lowenthal, Grijalva, and Barragán), for a total of 4 of 231 House Democrats.

The House referred it to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure committees on the day of introduction, and within two weeks it was referred to four subcommittees, including Water Resources and Environment and Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and fracking operators are better off: they never faced the federal disclosure, water replacement, air, and waste requirements the bill would have imposed, and drilling near homes and water supplies continues under the existing state-led rules and federal exemptions.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close oil and gas exemptions from federal water, air, and waste laws.

for.name: 4 of 231 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Lowenthal, Grijalva, Barragán and one original cosponsor recorded on the bill page)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members joined.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed federal fracking oversight of the kind this bill would impose, favoring state-level regulation and preservation of the 2005 drilling exemptions.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 4 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with narrow one-party support the bill never advanced in committee.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and fracking operators
industries.note: The bill strips the industry's exemptions from the Safe Drinking Water Act, Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, and hazardous waste rules, requires public chemical disclosure and baseline water testing, and makes operators replace contaminated water supplies. These provisions directly reverse the 2005-era carve-outs the industry obtained, so the industry's interest in the bill ran squarely against the drinking-water and air-quality interests of people living near wells.

The bill ends trade-secret protection for the identities and concentrations of chemicals injected underground and requires disclosure to states and the public, eliminating a confidentiality shield the suppliers had relied on.

industries.industry: Oil and gas waste disposal facilities
industries.note: Facilities receiving drilling fluids and produced water would face new groundwater monitoring, siting, corrective action, and financial assurance requirements under revised federal criteria, while the potential hazardous-waste listing could shift disposal demand among operators.
Geothermal is grouped with oil and gas in the underground injection and waste provisions, so it would face similar disclosure and waste requirements despite not being the bill's target.
